\chapter{Conclusion}

In the present contribution we study the sliding mode control (SMC) problem for a diffuse interface tumor growth model coupling a viscous Cahn-Hilliard type equation for the phase variable with a reaction-diffusion equation for the nutrient. First, we prove the well-posedness and some regularity results for the state system modified by the state-feedback control law. Then, we show that the chosen SMC law forces the system to reach within finite time the sliding manifold (that we chose in order that the tumor phase remains constant in time). The feedback control law is added in the Cahn-Hilliard type equation and leads the phase onto a prescribed target $\varphi^*$ in finite time.

\subsubsection *Key words:*

\paragraph*{Key words:}
sliding mode control, Cahn–Hilliard system, reaction-diffusion equation, tumor growth, nonlinear boundary value problem, state-feedback control law.

\subsection*{Custom particle dynamics}
A particle dynamics is automatic: it will always end with its current position being the relative ceiling of the cell; the diameters of the droplets along with their positions within the cell are left to the specification. We thus assess the state up to the moment at which it generates droplets any time a new droplet arrives a fixed distance. We thus assess only one second of its evolution. This point is then evaluated, with the default assumption that droplet sizes do not change with time. Typically, a cell might then have 2-4 sizes distributed between 64-128 nm in diameter.

Note
We thus averagely think of the cell, or rather a further treated cell, as having 3 size ranges, to account for the different scales of difference between distances and expected variations. We keep the parameterised cells in our model but evaluate its dynamics within regions balanced such that cell fluids are fluids until global variations are clumped within water boundaries, which occur several at most. This yields the formation of infinitesimal amounts of droplets.
\subsection*{Droplet dynamics}

process.The text then describes a process where at time \( t = T^* \), a particle with initial position \( x(t) = x_0(t) = 1 \) and velocity \( v(t) = 4 \ln(2) \) is being tracked through a closed curve.
